conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for coming in. I’m Dr. Lee, a perinatal mental-health clinician. My job is simply to listen and help you feel supported in these first weeks of motherhood.

Today we’ll use the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually called the EPDS. It’s a short, 10-question check-in about how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived. It helps us pick up on signs of depression or anxiety that can creep up after birth, so we can get you the right help early on.

Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me someone is in immediate danger. There are no right or wrong answers, and you can pause or skip anything. We’ll just chat through each question; most moms finish in under five minutes.

Ready to start? Here’s the first one:

Over the past seven days, how often have you found yourself able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

I’ve still been able to laugh—maybe not quite as easily as before the baby, but when my partner makes a silly face or when the dog does something goofy, I do find myself chuckling. I’d say most days I’ve had at least one good laugh.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yes, that’s me—I’ve been able to laugh and see the funny side of things.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
I do still look forward to little things—like my morning coffee or taking the baby out in the stroller when the weather’s nice. They’re small, but they feel good.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Not really. If the baby spits up a lot or won’t settle, I might think “maybe I ate something that bothered him” or “did I wait too long to swaddle?” but I don’t stay stuck on it. I figure babies just do these things and we’re both learning.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes I’ll suddenly wonder if the baby’s breathing when he’s napping, or I’ll worry that a tiny rash is something serious—even when everyone tells me it looks normal. It’s not constant, but yes, a couple of times this week I caught myself fretting when there wasn’t a real reason.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
No, I haven’t felt that kind of sudden fear or panic. A little anxious here and there, sure, but nothing that felt like a real scare or made my heart race for no reason.
Things have been getting on top of me

Not really. I mean, the days can feel busy and I’m definitely tired, but when I break things down—feed the baby, fold a load of laundry, take a shower—it all gets done without that “drowning” feeling people talk about.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, my sleep’s been okay. I go down pretty easily once the baby settles, and if I wake up it’s usually because he needs to eat, not because I’m feeling upset.
I have felt sad or miserable
I wouldn’t call it sad—more like a little “blah” once or twice when I was extra tired, but it passed quickly. Overall I’ve still had plenty of okay moments.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
No, I haven’t cried at all this week. Not even close to that kind of unhappy.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never—nothing like that has crossed my mind.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 5: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Patient-reported symptoms endorsed at above-threshold intensity:  
• Transient, situation-specific worry about infant well-being (Q4) – mild, non-persistent  
• Occasional “blah” mood when fatigued (Q8) – brief, self-limited  

Symptoms denied / below threshold:  
• Anhedonia or loss of pleasure (Q1, Q2)  
• Excessive or persistent guilt / self-blame (Q3)  
• Panic episodes, sense of overwhelm, or feeling “drowning” (Q5, Q6)  
• Mood-related insomnia, prolonged sadness, crying spells (Q7, Q8, Q9)  
• Self-harm ideation (Q10) – nil reported; no safety concern identified  

Pattern: Isolated, mild anxiety symptoms in setting of normal postpartum fatigue; no cluster suggesting major depressive or anxiety disorder at this time.

Screening conclusion: Low risk for current postpartum depression / anxiety; routine surveillance and psychosocial support recommended.
